prompt: Which of these statements can work as a standard rather than a guideline or a principle?
hint: Ask whether a reviewer could answer yes or no.

choices.text: Code should be easy to read
choices.why: Two reviewers would read it two ways; with no yes-or-no answer it is at most a weak guideline.

choices.text: No CPF number appears in a log line
choices.why: Right: a scanner, or any reviewer, can say yes or no, which is the test for a standard.

choices.text: Prefer PostgreSQL for new storage
choices.why: This is advice that accepts a different choice with a reason: a guideline, a should.

choices.text: Money moves through Payments and nowhere else
choices.why: A direction to reason from. It produces standards, but it cannot be checked line by line itself.

prompt: Renata asked seven tech leads to list Carreto's standards from memory. Nobody named more than five, and no two lists agreed. What did that show?
hint: A standard is worth what it prevents.

choices.text: That the tech leads had not read the wiki page carefully
choices.why: The lesson puts the failure on the page: sixty-one rules is more than anybody holds in their head while working.

choices.text: That each rule needed a longer explanation
choices.why: Longer rules make a list nobody reads even longer.

choices.text: That the page was not working as a set of standards
choices.why: Right: rules nobody remembers prevent nothing, so the page was a record of hopes rather than standards.

choices.text: That each team should keep its own list of standards
choices.why: Seven lists would make the disagreement official; the lists differing was the symptom, not the cure.

prompt: Why does every one of Carreto's nine standards carry a written reason?
hint: Think of an exception request, and of somebody reading the list in 2029.

choices.text: RFC 2119 asks for a reason beside each MUST
choices.why: RFC 2119 fixes what MUST and SHOULD mean; it says nothing about recording reasons.

choices.text: So that a broken rule points to who wrote it
choices.why: The owner answers questions about a standard; the reason is about why it exists, not about blame.

choices.text: So the page looks complete to an auditor
choices.why: Completeness for show is what the old wiki page had, and nobody followed it.

choices.text: To judge exceptions, and to know when to retire it
choices.why: Right: the reason tells an owner whether an exception makes sense and tells a later reader whether the rule is still needed.

prompt: A tech lead suggests that Renata, as the architect, should also own the logging standard, so that one person keeps all nine consistent. What fits the lesson?
hint: Who runs the logs and the scanner?

choices.text: Leave it with Paula, whose team runs the logs and the scanner
choices.why: Right: the owner answers questions and decides exceptions, so it should be the person closest to how the rule is checked.

choices.text: Accept, so that a single person answers for the whole list
choices.why: That makes the architect the gatekeeper lesson 17 describes: every exception waits for her.

choices.text: Give it to the tech leads as a group
choices.why: A group owner is nobody when a question or an exception arrives.

choices.text: Turn it into a guideline, since it has no clear owner
choices.why: It has a clear owner already, and it has a yes-or-no answer, so it stays a standard.

prompt: Match each kind of statement to Carreto's example of it.
hint: Must, should, and the direction both come from.

pairs.right: Money moves through Payments and nowhere else
Imports across team packages go through the api module

right_distractors: Every engineer reads the wiki once a quarter

prompt: Platform's service template meets five of the nine standards on a service's first day. What is the point of building it, by the lesson?
hint: The paved road.

choices.text: Teams are no longer allowed to start a service another way
choices.why: Leaving the road is allowed; the team then takes on what the template would have given it.

choices.text: Following the standards becomes less work than skipping them
choices.why: Right: the cheapest way to get a standard obeyed is to make obeying it the default.

choices.text: The list of standards can be deleted
choices.why: A team off the road still owes the nine, so the list stays.

choices.text: Platform can review each new service before it launches
choices.why: The template is about making the right thing easy, not adding a review step.

prompt: In the lesson's row of places where a broken standard is found, which places give the same answer for everybody?
hint: The left-hand group of the figure.

choices.text: Code review by a senior engineer
choices.why: Review depends on who happens to look, which is why the figure puts it on its own.

choices.text: Production monitoring
choices.why: By then the broken standard has already cost something; that is the end of the row the lesson wants to avoid.

choices.text: The editor, the commit and CI
choices.why: Right: those three are machines, so they check every change the same way, in seconds or minutes.

choices.text: The wiki page, where everybody can read the rule
choices.why: A rule on a wiki page is found by nobody until it costs something.

prompt: The import that broke the payouts had passed code review eleven months earlier. Why did review not catch it?
hint: Who could have known that offers.py was private?

choices.text: The reviewer that week was careless
choices.why: The lesson says nobody had been careless: the knowledge needed was in another team.

choices.text: Each team's review saw only its own side of the rule
choices.why: Right: the rule crossed two teams and each review saw only one side, which is the gap a machine closes.

choices.text: Reviews do not show import lines
choices.why: An import is an ordinary line of the diff; the problem was knowing it was wrong.

choices.text: The import was pushed to main without a pull request
choices.why: It went through review; the story depends on that.

prompt: What makes a check a fitness function rather than an ordinary unit test?
hint: The word the lesson says is the useful part of the idea.

choices.text: It runs in production instead of in CI
choices.why: That describes a continual one; a triggered fitness function runs in CI.

choices.text: The architect writes it instead of the team
choices.why: Who writes it is not what defines it.

choices.text: It needs a tool such as ArchUnit
choices.why: The lesson's checker uses the standard library only and is still a fitness function.

choices.text: It checks a property of the structure that no single function owns
choices.why: Right: a dependency rule, a latency budget or a time limit belongs to the architecture, not to one function.

prompt: Match each kind of fitness function to an example from Carreto.
hint: When it runs, and how many characteristics it looks at.

pairs.right: the import check on each pull request
an alert on quote latency in production
a load test measuring latency and error rate together

right_distractors: a design review in the architecture forum

prompt: The checker prints `allowed until 2027-03-31` for invoice.py. If nobody changes anything, what happens on 1 April 2027?
hint: Compare `today` with `until`.

choices.text: The exception is renewed for six months
choices.why: Nothing in the program renews anything; a renewal is a decision somebody makes and writes in.

choices.text: The line disappears from the output
choices.why: The import is still there, so the program still reports it, now as a violation.

choices.text: The import counts as a violation and the build fails
choices.why: Right: once today is past the date the exception no longer applies, so the run exits with 1.

choices.text: The program stops with an error about the date
choices.why: Comparing two ISO dates as strings works on any day; the program runs normally.

prompt: When check_imports.py finds a violation it exits with status ___, which is what turns a CI job red.
hint: The value `echo $?` printed after the failing run.

prompt: A file in carreto/payments writes `from carreto.matching import offers`. What does check_imports.py report?
hint: Work out `module` and `team_of(module)` for that line.

choices.text: It is flagged as a violation
choices.why: Right: `node.module` is `carreto.matching`, its team is matching, and only `carreto.matching.api` passes.

choices.text: Nothing, because it imports a package rather than a module inside it
choices.why: The check compares the module name, and `carreto.matching` is not the api module.

choices.text: Nothing, because from-imports are skipped
choices.why: `imports_in` reads `ImportFrom` nodes too; it skips only relative ones.

choices.text: A violation only if offers.py changed since the last run
choices.why: The check reads the code as it is; it has no memory of earlier runs.

prompt: The first run of the real check found 23 imports across team boundaries. Why did Renata freeze them in a baseline instead of failing the build?
hint: What would the teams have done with a red build that afternoon?

choices.text: So that the 23 became permanent exceptions
choices.why: A baseline only shrinks; entries leave and none are added.

choices.text: Failing at once would get the check switched off
choices.why: Right: freezing the current state and failing only on new violations brings the code to the rule without a week of blocked merges.

choices.text: Fitness functions are required to run in report-only mode
choices.why: Report-only was a first measurement, not a requirement; new violations failed from the first day.

choices.text: To give teams time to argue the standard down
choices.why: The baseline was a way to reach the rule, not to reopen it.

prompt: Carreto's baseline started with 23 imports and held 6 four months later. How many had been removed?
hint: A subtraction.

prompt: Put the life of Bruno's exception in order.
hint: From the ticket to the day after the date.
items: Bruno answers the five questions in a ticket
Renata checks the damage, the date and the person
The entry is added to EXCEPTIONS in a pull request
Every run prints the import as allowed until its date
After the date the build fails until something changes
trap: Recording the exception before the owner has judged it puts an undecided rule change into the code.

prompt: Why does Carreto record a granted exception in check_imports.py instead of in a spreadsheet beside the code?
hint: What happens on the day after the date, in each place?

choices.text: Spreadsheets cannot store dates reliably
choices.why: They can; the problem is that nothing reads the spreadsheet when the date passes.

choices.text: Only a pull request can carry Renata's approval
choices.why: Approval can be recorded in many places; the point is what happens at the expiry.

choices.text: It expires by itself when the build fails
choices.why: Right: nobody has to remember an exception the build remembers.

choices.text: It keeps the exception out of sight of other teams
choices.why: The opposite: the checker prints it on every run so it stays visible.

prompt: Who is named to close Bruno's exception?
hint: A person, not a team, and a deliberate choice.

choices.text: The Payments team
choices.why: A team as owner is nobody when the date arrives, which is why the request asks for a person.

choices.text: Ícaro Nunes
choices.why: Right: the junior who wrote invoice.py, so that talking to Tracking teaches him about boundaries.

choices.text: Renata, who owns the standard
choices.why: Renata decides the exception; closing it is the requester's side.

choices.text: The Tracking tech lead
choices.why: Tracking makes the api change, but the exception belongs to the code that imports.

prompt: Payments' nightly reconciliation job asked to be let off `/healthz` and `/metrics`. What did the lesson take from that request?
hint: The reason would hold for every job like it.

choices.text: The job should be rewritten as a web service so that it can comply with it
choices.why: That adds a server to a job that runs for twenty minutes, to satisfy wording.

choices.text: The standard assumed web services, so Paula split it into two rules
choices.why: Right: an exception whose reason holds for a whole kind of case is a finding about the standard.

choices.text: Granting it weakened the standard and should not have happened
choices.why: Refusing it would have protected the wording and lost the people.

choices.text: The job got a permanent exception
choices.why: Carreto's exceptions last six months at most; this one changed the standard instead.

prompt: Why does Renata's adoption table keep a column with the figures from six months earlier?
hint: 13 of 14: good or bad?

choices.text: A count alone cannot show progress or decline
choices.why: Right: without a starting point, 13 of 14 could be either.

choices.text: To show the board how much work the architect did
choices.why: The table measures standards, not the architect.

choices.text: Because a standard needs six months before it counts
choices.why: No rule says so; the column is about comparison.

choices.text: So that old exceptions can be renewed from it
choices.why: Renewal is decided on its own merits, per exception.

prompt: Diego proposes a new standard: "The Driver app's code should be well structured." Owner: "the mobile team". Checked by: "common sense". Which changes does the lesson call for? Choose all that apply.
hint: Rule, reason, owner, check.

choices.text: Rewrite it so a reviewer can answer yes or no
choices.why: Yes: as written, two reviewers would read it two ways.

choices.text: Name one person as its owner
choices.why: Yes: a team as owner is nobody when an exception is asked for.

choices.text: Add it to the wiki page so that everybody can see it
choices.why: A rule on a page is what Carreto had sixty-one of; visibility is not checking.

choices.text: Write down the reason and how it will be checked
choices.why: Yes: without a reason it cannot be judged or retired, and without a check it is found in production.

prompt: An exception at Carreto has been renewed four times. What does the lesson say it has become?
hint: At most one renewal, and why.

choices.text: A stable arrangement that has proved itself
choices.why: Four renewals prove the date was never real.

choices.text: Noise in the CI log that should move to a spreadsheet
choices.why: Moving it out of the check is how exceptions get forgotten.

choices.text: A second standard nobody wrote down
choices.why: Right: after a year either the code meets the standard or the standard changes.

choices.text: A reason to remove the check
choices.why: One stale exception says something about that case, not about the check.

prompt: The first log scanner flagged every eleven-digit number as a CPF, order references included. Why did fixing it in the second week matter, by the lesson?
hint: What people do after a few false alarms.

choices.text: The scanner was slowing the pipeline down
choices.why: The lesson's concern is what wrong failures teach people, not speed.

choices.text: Order references count as personal data under the LGPD as well
choices.why: They were the false positives, not the target.

choices.text: A wrong alarm counts as an exception and expires
choices.why: False alarms are not exceptions; nobody asked for them.

choices.text: False failures teach people to rerun builds without reading
choices.why: Right: after a few, the check stops being read even when it is right.
